items.stem: According to the GSMA, in low- and middle-income countries women are less likely than men to use mobile internet. Roughly how much less likely (2024 report)?
items.answer: About 15%
items.markingKey: About 15%. The GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report 2024 estimated a 15% gap.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Giving every student a laptop closes the digital divide." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Devices without connectivity, maintenance, teacher training and relevant content may have little effect; One Laptop per Child evaluations in Peru found no significant improvement in maths or reading.
items.markingKey: Devices without connectivity, maintenance, teacher training and relevant content may have little effect; One Laptop per Child evaluations in Peru found no significant improvement in maths or reading. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the first-level digital divide and the second-level digital divide.
items.answer: The first level concerns physical access to devices and connectivity; the second concerns skills and how effectively people use that access.
items.markingKey: The first level concerns physical access to devices and connectivity; the second concerns skills and how effectively people use that access. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A survey in a Latin American country found that 82% of households in the richest fifth and 48% of households in the poorest fifth used the internet in the last three months. Calculate the gap in percentage points.
items.answer: 34 percentage points
items.markingKey: 82 − 48 = 34 percentage points [A1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which One Laptop per Child in Peru shows why access alone does not close the divide.
items.answer: Peru distributed hundreds of thousands of low-cost XO laptops from 2008; an Inter-American Development Bank evaluation found no significant effect on maths or reading scores. Devices without teacher training, connectivity and integration into teaching did not improve learning outcomes.
items.markingKey: Context (Peru distributed hundreds of thousands of low-cost XO laptops from 2008; an Inter-American Development Bank evaluation found no significant effect on maths or reading scores.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: devices without teacher training, connectivity and integration into teaching did not improve learning outcomes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to why access alone does not close the divide.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"My daughter does her homework on my phone after I come home from work, using the data that is left."
— Parent in Mexico City, interviewed for a 2021 study on remote learning

Explain how the source illustrates more than one level of the digital divide.
items.answer: Access: a single shared phone and limited data (first level); use: homework is limited by time and device suitability (second level); outcomes: the child may learn less than peers with laptops and broadband (third level).
items.markingKey: Access: a single shared phone and limited data (first level); use: homework is limited by time and device suitability (second level); outcomes: the child may learn less than peers with laptops and broadband (third level). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Analyse the causes of the digital divide in one country or community you have studied and evaluate one intervention designed to reduce it.
items.answer: Causes: cost, infrastructure, skills, language, gender norms, disability; intervention e.g. BharatNet, Giga school connectivity, public Wi-Fi, digital skills training, device schemes; evaluate effectiveness and stakeholders.
items.markingKey: Causes: cost, infrastructure, skills, language, gender norms, disability; intervention e.g. BharatNet, Giga school connectivity, public Wi-Fi, digital skills training, device schemes; evaluate effectiveness and stakeholders.

items.stem: "Governments, not companies, should be responsible for closing the digital divide." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Governments should lead and set targets, but closing the divide needs partnerships with companies and civil society.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: access is a public good linked to rights and services; markets under-serve poor and rural areas. Arguments against: companies drive infrastructure and cheaper devices; public–private partnerships (BharatNet, Giga) combine strengths; civil society delivers skills training. Supported judgement: Governments should lead and set targets, but closing the divide needs partnerships with companies and civil society. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The gap between men and women in access to and use of digital technologies"?
items.answer: gender digital divide
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of gender digital divide.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the digital divide can deepen existing inequalities.
items.answer: As jobs, education, banking and government services move online, those without access or skills are excluded from opportunities and information, so the disadvantaged fall further behind.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: As jobs, education, banking and government services move online, those without access or skills are excluded from opportunities and information, so the disadvantaged fall further behind. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why women in many countries have lower access to mobile internet than men.
items.answer: Barriers include affordability (lower incomes), literacy and digital skills, social norms and family restrictions on phone use, and concerns about safety and harassment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Barriers include affordability (lower incomes), literacy and digital skills, social norms and family restrictions on phone use, and concerns about safety and harassment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tomás writes: "The digital divide only exists in low-income countries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: High-income countries also have divides by income, age, disability and rurality – e.g. students in the US "homework gap" lacking home broadband during COVID-19.
items.markingKey: High-income countries also have divides by income, age, disability and rurality – e.g. students in the US "homework gap" lacking home broadband during COVID-19. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using remote learning during COVID-19 as an example, explain the digital divide in education.
items.answer: UNICEF estimated that at least 463 million schoolchildren could not be reached by remote learning when schools closed in 2020. Unequal access to devices, connectivity and support turned school closures into unequal learning losses, deepening educational inequality.
items.markingKey: Context (UNICEF estimated that at least 463 million schoolchildren could not be reached by remote learning when schools closed in 2020.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: unequal access to devices, connectivity and support turned school closures into unequal learning losses, deepening educational inequality. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the digital divide in education.

items.stem: A survey in a Latin American country found that 80% of people aged 16–24 and 45% of people aged 65 and over have a broadband connection at home. Calculate the gap in percentage points and, if there are 2,000,000 people aged 65 and over, how many of them do not.
items.answer: 35 percentage points; 1,100,000 people aged 65 and over

items.answer: Governments should lead and set targets, but closing the divide needs partnerships with companies and civil society.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "embodied carbon"?
options: The greenhouse-gas emissions produced in extracting materials, manufacturing and transporting a product before it is used
Software that converts on-screen text and interface elements into speech or braille, such as JAWS, NVDA or VoiceOver
Minerals such as tin, tantalum (from coltan), tungsten and gold mined in conflict areas, where profits may fund armed groups
The skills needed to find, evaluate, create and communicate information using digital technologies safely and effectively
items.answer: The greenhouse-gas emissions produced in extracting materials, manufacturing and transporting a product before it is used
items.markingKey: A. "embodied carbon" is the greenhouse-gas emissions produced in extracting materials, manufacturing and transporting a product before it is used.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Digital technology is environmentally friendly because it is "virtual"." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Digital services depend on physical devices, mining, data centres and networks that use energy, water and minerals and create e-waste.
items.markingKey: Digital services depend on physical devices, mining, data centres and networks that use energy, water and minerals and create e-waste. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between informal recycling and formal recycling.
items.answer: Formal recycling uses regulated facilities with safety and pollution controls; informal recycling is unregulated work, often burning or acid-stripping components, which harms workers and the environment.
items.markingKey: Formal recycling uses regulated facilities with safety and pollution controls; informal recycling is unregulated work, often burning or acid-stripping components, which harms workers and the environment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A school has 30 computers, each using 400 W, switched on for 6 hours a day on 250 days a year. Calculate the annual electricity use in kWh.

Read the source below.

"The greenest phone is the one you already own."
— Slogan used by repair campaigners, e.g. Restart Project, UK

Explain the argument in the source.
items.answer: Because most emissions come from manufacturing, keeping and repairing existing devices avoids the embodied carbon and resources of making new ones.
items.markingKey: Because most emissions come from manufacturing, keeping and repairing existing devices avoids the embodied carbon and resources of making new ones. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Evaluate one intervention designed to reduce the environmental impact of computing devices.
items.answer: E.g. EU common charger (USB-C, 2024), right-to-repair rules, WEEE producer responsibility, Fairphone, Apple trade-in; analyse effects on e-waste and emissions, stakeholders, limitations; judgement.
items.markingKey: E.g. EU common charger (USB-C, 2024), right-to-repair rules, WEEE producer responsibility, Fairphone, Apple trade-in; analyse effects on e-waste and emissions, stakeholders, limitations; judgement.

items.stem: Define the term "planned obsolescence".
items.answer: Designing products to have a limited useful life or to become outdated so that consumers replace them
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: designing products to have a limited useful life or to become outdated so that consumers replace them. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the growth of AI is increasing concern about the environmental impact of computing.
items.answer: Training and running large AI models require huge numbers of GPUs in data centres that consume large amounts of electricity and water for cooling, so demand for energy and hardware is rising quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Training and running large AI models require huge numbers of GPUs in data centres that consume large amounts of electricity and water for cooling, so demand for energy and hardware is rising quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why most of the carbon footprint of a smartphone occurs before it is used.
items.answer: Mining metals, manufacturing chips and screens and global transport use large amounts of energy, while a phone uses little electricity when charging, so manufacturing (embodied carbon) dominates its lifetime emissions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mining metals, manufacturing chips and screens and global transport use large amounts of energy, while a phone uses little electricity when charging, so manufacturing (embodied carbon) dominates its lifetime emissions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Agbogbloshie, Accra, explain how it illustrates environmental and social impacts of e-waste.
items.answer: For years workers, including children, at Agbogbloshie burned cables and dismantled imported electronics to recover copper and other metals, exposing themselves to toxic fumes; the site was demolished by the authorities in 2021. The costs of global electronics consumption were borne by informal workers in a low-income country, illustrating environmental injustice.
items.markingKey: Context (For years workers, including children, at Agbogbloshie burned cables and dismantled imported electronics to recover copper and other metals, exposing themselves to toxic fumes; the site was demolished by the authorities in 2021.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the costs of global electronics consumption were borne by informal workers in a low-income country, illustrating environmental injustice. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to environmental and social impacts of e-waste.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The environmental costs of digital technology outweigh its environmental benefits."
items.answer: Digital technology can support sustainability, but only if its own footprint is managed through renewable energy, longer device lifetimes and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: e-waste, mining and data-centre energy; rapidly rising AI electricity demand. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.markingKey: 4.5:1. Large text needs 3:1; AAA requires 7:1.

items.stem: "Adding a screen reader to a computer makes every website accessible." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Screen readers depend on websites being coded accessibly (alt text, labels, headings); poorly built sites remain unusable even with assistive technology.
items.markingKey: Screen readers depend on websites being coded accessibly (alt text, labels, headings); poorly built sites remain unusable even with assistive technology. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Domino's Pizza accessibility case (USA), explain how it illustrates legal pressure for digital accessibility.
items.answer: A blind customer, Guillermo Robles, sued Domino's because its website and app did not work with his screen reader; in 2019 the US Supreme Court declined to hear Domino's appeal, letting the case proceed. The case signalled that the Americans with Disabilities Act can apply to websites and apps, pushing businesses to follow WCAG.
items.markingKey: Context (A blind customer, Guillermo Robles, sued Domino's because its website and app did not work with his screen reader; in 2019 the US Supreme Court declined to hear Domino's appeal, letting the case proceed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Nothing about us without us."
— Slogan of the disability rights movement, popularised by James Charlton (1998)

Explain how this source applies to the design of digital technology.
items.answer: Disabled people should be involved in designing technologies meant for them, because they understand the barriers best; inclusive design should be co-designed rather than imposed.
items.markingKey: Disabled people should be involved in designing technologies meant for them, because they understand the barriers best; inclusive design should be co-designed rather than imposed. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Accessibility should be a legal requirement for all websites."
items.answer: Legal requirements are justified and effective when supported by guidance and proportionate expectations for small organisations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ensures equal rights (CRPD); the European Accessibility Act applies from June 2025. Arguments against: costs for small businesses; enforcement challenges; guidelines may be applied as box-ticking. Supported judgement: Legal requirements are justified and effective when supported by guidance and proportionate expectations for small organisations.

items.stem: Explain why inclusive design benefits people without disabilities.
items.answer: Features such as captions, voice control and high contrast help people in noisy places, people learning a language, older users or anyone using a phone in sunlight – the curb-cut effect.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Features such as captions, voice control and high contrast help people in noisy places, people learning a language, older users or anyone using a phone in sunlight – the curb-cut effect. items.stem: Distinguish between accessibility and usability.
items.answer: Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, use and understand a product; usability is how easy and efficient a product is for its users in general – accessible design usually improves usability.
items.markingKey: Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, use and understand a product; usability is how easy and efficient a product is for its users in general – accessible design usually improves usability. items.answer: December 2024

"Access to the internet is no longer a luxury. It is a prerequisite for participating in society, the economy and democracy."

items.stem: A smartphone causes about 85 kg CO₂e in manufacturing and about 8 kg CO₂e per year in use. Calculate the average emissions per year of use if it is kept for 3 years and for 5 years, and state what this suggests about device lifetimes.
items.answer: 36.3 kg/yr vs 25.0 kg/yr; keeping devices longer spreads manufacturing emissions, so longer lifetimes (repair, right to repair) reduce impact
items.markingKey: (85 + 8×3) ÷ 3 = 36.3 [M1 A1]; (85 + 8×5) ÷ 5 = 25.0 [A1]; most emissions are from manufacturing, so longer use reduces annual impact [R1].

"Solve for one, extend to many."

items.stem: Explain why e-waste is often exported to lower-income countries.
items.answer: Formal recycling is expensive in high-income countries, and used electronics can be exported labelled as "second-hand goods"; informal recyclers in places such as Ghana or Pakistan recover metals cheaply, often unsafely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Formal recycling is expensive in high-income countries, and used electronics can be exported labelled as "second-hand goods"; informal recyclers in places such as Ghana or Pakistan recover metals cheaply, often unsafely. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why accessibility is described as a human-rights issue.
items.answer: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) requires access to information and communications technology; inaccessible digital services exclude disabled people from education, work and public life.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) requires access to information and communications technology; inaccessible digital services exclude disabled people from education, work and public life. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the mobile gender gap and explain what it reveals about the gender digital divide.
items.answer: GSMA reports show women in low- and middle-income countries are less likely than men to use mobile internet, with the widest gaps in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Affordability, skills and social norms limit women's access, reducing their access to information, finance and work.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"In 2022, 62 million tonnes of e-waste were produced globally; only 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled."
— Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (ITU and UNITAR)

With reference to the source, explain one implication of these figures.
items.answer: Most e-waste is not formally recycled, so valuable materials are lost and toxic substances may pollute the environment or harm informal recyclers; this suggests the need for better collection, repair and producer responsibility.
items.markingKey: Most e-waste is not formally recycled, so valuable materials are lost and toxic substances may pollute the environment or harm informal recyclers; this suggests the need for better collection, repair and producer responsibility. items.stem: Outline one way in which the Xbox Adaptive Controller shows inclusive design.
items.answer: Microsoft designed the 2018 controller with gamers with limited mobility and charities such as AbleGamers; it connects to switches, buttons and joysticks. Designing with disabled users from the start produced a mainstream product that widened participation in gaming culture.

Calculate the gap in percentage points and, if there are 8,000,000 households in the poorest fifth, how many of them do not.
items.answer: 21 percentage points; 3,120,000 households in the poorest fifth

items.stem: Using Agbogbloshie, Accra as an example, explain environmental and social impacts of e-waste.
items.answer: For years workers, including children, at Agbogbloshie burned cables and dismantled imported electronics to recover copper and other metals, exposing themselves to toxic fumes; the site was demolished by the authorities in 2021. The costs of global electronics consumption were borne by informal workers in a low-income country, illustrating environmental injustice.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The environmental costs of digital technology outweigh its environmental benefits."
items.answer: Digital technology can support sustainability, but only if its own footprint is managed through renewable energy, longer device lifetimes and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: e-waste, mining and data-centre energy; rapidly rising AI electricity demand. Arguments against: smart grids, remote working and dematerialisation can cut emissions; environmental monitoring by satellites and sensors; efficiency gains (PUE improvements). Supported judgement: Digital technology can support sustainability, but only if its own footprint is managed through renewable energy, longer device lifetimes and recycling.

items.stem: "Digital technology has done more to include than exclude people with disabilities." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Digital technology has greatly widened possibilities, but inclusion depends on accessible design being required and enforced.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: screen readers, voice assistants and captions open access to information and work; remote work and online services reduce physical barriers. Arguments against: many websites still fail basic accessibility (WebAIM finds most home pages have errors); new technologies (CAPTCHAs, touch-only interfaces) create barriers; cost of assistive devices. Supported judgement: Digital technology has greatly widened possibilities, but inclusion depends on accessible design being required and enforced. items.stem: "Governments, not companies, should be responsible for closing the digital divide." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Governments should lead and set targets, but closing the divide needs partnerships with companies and civil society.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: access is a public good linked to rights and services; markets under-serve poor and rural areas. Arguments against: companies drive infrastructure and cheaper devices; public–private partnerships (BharatNet, Giga) combine strengths; civil society delivers skills training.
